The dispute is between the Count of Flanders (unmatched) and the French crown over the count's ransom/release terms and obligations not to act against the king or his lands. Louis VIII (matched) appears as the principal lay party whose interests are being protected; Philip II Augustus (matched) is mentioned only as the deceased father who originally made the agreement with the count.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Martin IV grants a privilege to King Philip III of France, allowing royal clerks who study at the University of Paris (with royal permission) to continue receiving the revenues and income of their benefices as if they were personally resident in their churches, with the exception of daily distributions. This is a one-sided papal indult/grace addressed to the king, with no opposing party. Philip III appears as the addressee and beneficiary of the grant.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe IV, Roi de France (addressee) | Edward I 'Longshanks', King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Boniface VIII sends a formal remonstrance (admonition) to King Philip IV of France, rebuking him for issuing an ordinance that the pope believes infringes upon ecclesiastical liberty — specifically regarding the property and persons of the Church within France. This is a one-sided papal letter of admonition, not a live litigation or arbitration between two parties; the pope is reproving the king for his conduct, but no formal dispute proceeding is operative. Philip IV is the addressee and subject of the rebuke; Edward I of England appears only as an incidental mention in the broader text.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe IV, Roi de France (addressee) | Edward I 'Longshanks', King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Boniface VIII writes to Philip IV of France to clarify that, beyond what has already been pronounced, he will not proceed to any further sentence or definition in the matter of peace and concord between Philip IV and Edward I of England without Philip's express prior consent given by letters patent and special messenger. The document concerns an ongoing arbitration/dispute between the two kings over peace terms, with Boniface acting as private arbitrator. Both matched persons are principals: Philip IV as addressee/party to the arbitration, and Edward I as the opposing party.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe IV, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Boniface VIII writes to Pierre Flotte, counsellor of King Philip IV of France, requesting his assistance in ensuring that the undistributed goods of the late Cardinal John of Santa Cecilia are properly restored and assigned to Cardinal John of Saints Marcellinus and Peter (or his representative). The document concerns the administration of a deceased cardinal's estate, with papal executors having arrested/detained certain goods in France. Philip IV is mentioned only incidentally as Pierre Flotte's lord; there is no live dispute between opposing parties — this is a solicitation/request regarding the pious disposition of a cardinal's goods.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Robert d'Anjou, King of Naples (addressee) | Charles II d'Anjou, King of Naples (subject_or_mention) | Frederico II d'Aragona-Sicilia, Re di Sicilia (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Boniface VIII grants a crusade-equivalent plenary indulgence to Charles of Valois, Count of Anjou, and his troops (cavalry and infantry) for their military campaign to recover the Kingdom of Sicily against Frederick of Aragon and his rebel allies. The document frames the Sicilian campaign as equivalent to a crusade to the Holy Land, granting the same indulgence as that conceded at the general council for those crossing the sea in aid of the Holy Land. The matched persons are: Charles of Valois (addressee/principal beneficiary of the grant), Charles II of Anjou (King of Sicily, named as the aggrieved party), and Frederick II of Aragon-Sicily (the rebel opponent). Note: the Peerage match for the addressee appears to be Robert d'Anjou rather than Charles of Valois, but the document is clearly addressed to "Carolo comiti Andegavensi" (Charles of Valois).

persons: Louis VIII, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Honorius III announces to the prelates of France and Provence the dispatch of his legate Romano to the province of Narbonne, describing the deplorable religious and political state of that region (likely referring to the Albigensian heresy). This is a circular letter of notification, not a dispute proceeding. Louis VIII of France is mentioned incidentally as the reigning king, not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee) | Philippe II Auguste Capet, Roi de France (subject_or_mention) | Louis VIII, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to King Louis IX of France asking him not to hear the Queen of Cyprus (Aalidis/Alice) in her claim to the succession of the County of Champagne until the causa natalium (legitimacy/birth status case) concerning her has been decided by the Apostolic See. The dispute is between the Queen of Cyprus (lay claimant) and the succession to Champagne, with the Church asserting jurisdiction over the preliminary legitimacy question. Louis IX appears as the addressee being instructed; Philippe II Auguste and Louis VIII are mentioned as having received a similar request from Honorius III.

persons: Blanca de Castilla (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Gregory IX mandates the Archbishop of Sens to examine and potentially dispense or commute certain vows rashly made by Queen Blanche of France (Blanca de Castilla), who had petitioned the pope for relief. This is a one-sided administrative/pastoral act with no opposing party. The matched Peerage person, Blanca de Castilla, appears as the beneficiary/petitioner of the dispensation.

persons: Friedrich I 'Barbarossa' Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Alexander III writes to the consuls and men of the Lombard League cities (Lombardy, Marche, Romagna) to strengthen their alliance against Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. The document concerns the active political and military conflict between the Lombard League (lay communes) and the Emperor, with the papacy supporting the League. Frederick I Barbarossa appears only as the named adversary/subject of the conflict, not as a matched principal party; the actual addressees and principals are the Lombard League consuls (unmatched) and the Pope himself.

persons: Friedrich II von Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius III notifies the rectors of the Second Lombard League of the peace terms they must observe with Emperor Frederick II. The document records an active papal mediation/arbitration of a live conflict between the Lombard League (lay communes) and Emperor Frederick II (lay ruler), with both parties having submitted the matter to the pope's disposition. Frederick II is the matched Peerage person and a principal party to the dispute; the Lombard League rectors are the unmatched counterparty.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Friedrich II von Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius III notifies Emperor Frederick II of the peace terms he must observe with the Lombard League (the society of Lombardy, Romagna, and the March). The document is an active papal mediation/brokering of a live conflict between Frederick II and the Lombard League, including the form letter Frederick must send to the League's rectors. Frederick II is the matched addressee and a principal party; the Lombard League (an unmatched collective) is the counterparty.

summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to King Ferdinand III of Castile and León urging him to make peace or conclude a truce with King Thibaut IV of Navarre. The letter frames the ongoing conflict between the two Christian rulers as harmful to the general Church and especially to the cause of the Holy Land/crusade. Ferdinand III is the addressee/principal, and Thibaut IV of Navarre is the other principal party to the dispute.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Celestine III writes to Sancho VI (the Wise), King of Navarre, urging him to restore the castle of San Esteban and to receive back into his favour Juan de Tarazona, archdeacon of Pamplona, and Fortún, prior of Alo. The dispute is between the king (lay) and these two ecclesiastics, who had appealed to the Holy See in defence of the rights of the church of Pamplona. Sancho VII of Navarre is the matched addressee and principal party; the ecclesiastical counterparties (Juan de Tarazona and Fortún) are unmatched.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee) | Alfonso VIII, Rey de Castilla (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Celestine III writes to Sancho VII of Navarre (the addressee/principal), exhorting him to renounce his treaty and annual tribute arrangement with the Saracens and instead join the Christian kings of Castile and Aragon in fighting against them. The operative conflict is between Christian rulers and the Saracens (Muslims), with the pope urging Sancho to abandon his alliance with the enemy of the faith. Alfonso VIII of Castile is mentioned as one of the Christian kings Sancho should ally with, not as a party to a dispute.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Celestine III instructs his legate Cardinal Gregory of Sant'Angelo (and, in his absence, the bishops of Tarragona, Tarazona, and Calahorra) to pressure Sancho VII of Navarre to break his alliance with the Muslim enemies of the faith and join the Christian kings in fighting the Saracens. The pope also reports having written to the kings of Castile and Aragon to make peace with Navarre, exchanging castles as pledges, and then wage war together against the Saracens, dividing any conquests among themselves. Sancho VII of Navarre appears as the subject of the mandate — the party to be admonished — not as a matched principal in a formal legal dispute; the operative matter is a papally-brokered crusading coalition and peace among Christian rulers directed against Muslim forces.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent III writes to Sancho VII, King of Navarre, admonishing him for having destroyed the hospital of San Miguel in Pamplona, where many poor were cared for. The pope urges the king to make amends for this act. This is not a formal dispute but a papal exhortation/mandate directed at the king as the sole responsible party. Sancho VII is the addressee and the principal subject of the letter.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Honorius III confirms to Sancho VII, King of Navarre, possession of Castillo Nuevo and several other castles (Alcedo, Allocaf, Mallen, Peña de Arañon, Arcediello, Avengalbon) acquired on the Saracen frontier, as well as any future fortifications he may build there. This is a straightforward apostolic confirmation of secular territorial possessions, with no opposing party named. Sancho VII is the addressee and sole principal.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius III exhorts Sancho VII, King of Navarre, to support the poor of the hospital of Roncesvalles and to protect the goods granted to it by the faithful. This is a one-sided exhortatory letter with no live dispute; the pope urges the king to follow the example of his royal predecessors who founded the hospital. Sancho VII appears as the sole addressee and principal recipient of the papal admonition.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius III writes to Sancho VII of Navarre (the matched person, as addressee) asking him to continue his patronage of the canons of Roncesvalles and to have the church he had built at his own expense consecrated. This is a one-sided papal request/mandate, not a live dispute between parties. Sancho VII appears as the addressee and benefactor being urged to protect the Roncesvalles community.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius III writes to King Sancho VII of Navarre on behalf of the prior and brothers of the Hospital of Roncesvalles, asking the king to continue favouring them despite accusations (apparently false) that they had tried to strip him of his right of patronage over the hospital by obtaining an exemption privilege from the pope. The document is a papal intercession/recommendation letter, not a live dispute before a tribunal. Sancho VII (matched) is the addressee; the brothers of Roncesvalles are the beneficiaries of the pope's plea.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention) | Jaime I, Rey de AragÃ³n (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius III instructs the Archbishop of Toledo (papal legate) to protect the kingdom of Navarre and its king, Sancho VII, who has taken the Cross against the Moors of Spain. The pope orders the archbishop to restrain, after due warning, anyone who presumes to invade Sancho's rights or disturb his kingdom while he is occupied on crusade. A condition is added that Sancho and his men must not offend King James I of Aragon or his kingdom during the expedition. Both Sancho VII and James I appear as subjects of the mandate, not as disputants against each other.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (requestor)
summary: Pope Honorius III mandates the abbots of Fitero and Veruela and the prior of Nájera to compel A. de Luna and other laymen of the dioceses of Zaragoza, Tarazona, and Calahorra to make reparations to King Sancho VII of Navarre for damages inflicted on his lands and men while he was fighting against the Moors under apostolic protection. The dispute is between Sancho VII (matched, requestor/principal) and A. de Luna and associates (unmatched lay aggressors). The document concerns a live conflict over hostile incursions into the king's territory during his crusading campaign against the Moors.

persons: Sancho VII, Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory IX instructs Sancho VII, King of Navarre, to compel the Jews of his kingdom to wear distinctive clothing separating them from Christians, as decreed by the Fourth Lateran Council, under pain of withdrawal of Christian fellowship. This is a one-sided papal mandate directed at the king, with no opposing party or live dispute. Sancho VII is the addressee and sole matched principal, tasked with enforcing the canonical statute against the Jews of Navarre.
domain_other_detail: Enforcement of canonical statute requiring Jews to wear distinctive dress

persons: Raimond IV de Saint-Gilles, Comte de Toulouse (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Urban II grants a solemn privilege to the canons of Saint-Sernin de Toulouse, confirming their rights to altar oblations and other church portions following a dispute with Bishop Ysarn of Toulouse, which was settled by synodal judgment in the pope's presence. The bishop renounced his claim to the quarter-share of oblations before the pope and the canons. The matched Peerage person, Count Raymond IV of Toulouse, appears only incidentally as having renounced certain rights at the church's dedication ceremony, not as a principal party to the dispute.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory IX grants a crusade protection privilege to Thibaut IV, King of Navarre and Count of Champagne, who has taken the cross and intends to go on crusade to the Holy Land. The operative act is a grant of immunity from excommunication or interdict by ordinary or delegated authority without special mandate of the Apostolic See, to last until his return or death is confirmed. Thibaut IV is the sole principal party as the addressee and beneficiary of this privilege.

persons: Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Gregory IX mandates all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates to ensure that no one hinders or disturbs the king of Navarre (Thibaut I/IV, also count of Champagne) as he travels through their jurisdictions on his way to the Holy Land, having taken the cross. This is a crusade protection letter, not a live dispute between parties. Thibaut I is the matched Peerage person and the subject of the protection, appearing as the crusader whose passage is to be safeguarded.

persons: Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX issues a letter to all dukes, counts, barons, and faithful Christians recommending safe passage and assistance for King Thibaut I of Navarre (Count of Champagne), who has taken the cross and is preparing to depart on crusade to the Holy Land. The pope urges all recipients to receive the king and his men hospitably and provide them secure conduct through their lands. Thibaut I of Navarre is the principal subject of the letter, appearing as the crusader being commended.

persons: Jaime I, Rey de AragÃ³n (addressee) | Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to King James I of Aragon (matched, addressee) requesting that he receive the King of Navarre (Thibaut I/IV, matched, mentioned) and his retinue safely through Aragonese territory as they travel to the Holy Land on crusade. This is a one-sided papal letter of instruction/request, not a live dispute. The operative act is facilitating a crusade passage, making the dominant domain crusade.

persons: Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to the community of Marseille requesting that they receive and provide safe conduct to Thibaut I (King of Navarre, Count of Champagne) and his men as they pass through on their way to the Holy Land on crusade. This is a one-sided papal letter of recommendation/request, not a dispute. Thibaut I is the subject of the letter, mentioned as the crusader whose passage is to be facilitated.

persons: Guglielmo II di Sicilia, Re di Sicilia (addressee)
summary: Pope Alexander III issues a privilege to King William II of Sicily, promoting the newly founded monastery of Santa Maria Nova di Monreale to the status of a full nullius abbey. The document grants the abbey independence from all ecclesiastical authority except the Holy See, confirms all its properties, grants full episcopal ordination rights to the archbishop, and bestows the use of full episcopal insignia on the abbot. This is a one-sided papal grant/confirmation with no opposing party; William II is the addressee and founding patron of the abbey.

persons: Friedrich I von Habsburg, Holy Roman Emperor (addressee)
summary: Pope Clement V writes to Duke Friedrich I of Austria (Habsburg), ordering him to arrest any Templars in his territories who have not yet been captured, hand them over to local ordinaries or inquisitors, and assist in the inquisition proceedings against them. This is a mandate related to the suppression of the Knights Templar, not a bilateral dispute. Friedrich I appears as the addressee and target of the papal instruction.

persons: Blanca de Castilla (addressee) | Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention) | Friedrich II von Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to Queen Blanche of Castile (matched, addressee) commending the Bishop of Palestrina (Jacobus), whom he is sending as papal legate to France for the defense of the Catholic faith. The letter urges Blanche to persuade her son Louis IX (matched, mentioned) to receive the legate warmly and support the apostolic cause, explicitly framing this against the deceptions of Emperor Frederick II (matched, mentioned as adversary of the Church). This is a one-sided exhortatory letter — a commendation of the legate — with no live dispute being adjudicated; the conflict with Frederick II is cited as background context motivating the legation, not as an operative matter before the pope.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to King Louis IX of France on behalf of Joffrid de Grand Pré, elect of Châlons-sur-Marne. The pope explains that he has revoked to apostolic examination the appeals lodged against the elect (who had been confirmed by the Archbishop of Reims), and has ruled that the treasurer of Châlons may not pursue those appeals further. Gregory urges Louis IX to restore the regalia of the church of Châlons and the fruits collected since the confirmation to the elect. Louis IX appears as the addressee/principal, asked to act in favour of the elect against the obstruction of the treasurer of Châlons (an unmatched ecclesiastical party).

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to King Louis IX of France urging him to restore the regalia (temporal investiture) to the bishop-elect of Châlons-sur-Marne (Cathalaunensis ecclesia). This is not a live dispute before the papal court but rather a papal exhortation/instruction to the king to carry out a restitution already adjudicated by Gregory IX. Louis IX appears as the addressee and principal recipient of the papal mandate.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to King Louis IX of France to commend Stephen, nephew of the Roman citizen John Timosus, regarding a prebend in the church of Constance. The prebend had been canonically conferred on Stephen by the bishop and canons of Constance per papal mandate, but was then seized by Master Robert de Campellis under the pretext that the collation belonged to the king. Louis IX appears as addressee being asked to support Stephen's cause; the real dispute is between Stephen (and the papacy) on one side and Master Robert de Campellis on the other.

persons: Raimond VII, Comte de Toulouse (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Innocent IV mandates the Archbishop of Bari to absolve Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, from all sentences of excommunication (including one issued by Dominican inquisitors Ferrarius and G. Raymundi) as a precautionary measure ("ad cautelam"), upon receipt of his sworn oath to obey apostolic mandates. The document concerns the operative act of lifting excommunication censures from the Count of Toulouse. Raymond VII is the matched principal beneficiary; the Archbishop of Bari is the addressee/executor, and the Dominican inquisitors are the unmatched ecclesiastical counterparty who had issued the sentence.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV grants King Louis IX of France (the matched addressee) the faculty to choose one of his chaplains as a personal confessor, empowered to absolve him from excommunications he has incurred or may incur in the future, except those pronounced by special mandate of the Apostolic See or involving grave and enormous offences requiring papal consultation. This is a one-sided privilege/indulgence granted to Louis IX with no opposing party. The operative act is a clerical/spiritual faculty (confessor privilege) granted to a lay ruler.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to King Louis IX of France requesting that he compel Peter de Acis (Pierre d'Aix), then seneschal of the king at Beaucaire, to make restitution to Thomas de Pinasca, a Genoese citizen, who was allegedly stripped of his ship and goods worth 70 Tournois livres without reasonable cause while sailing along the Provençal coast. The dispute is between Thomas de Pinasca (lay, Genoese) and Peter de Acis (lay, royal official); Louis IX appears only as the addressee being asked to intervene. The operative act is a papal intercession in a secular property/injury dispute between two lay parties.
domain_other_detail: secular property seizure / restitution claim between lay parties

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to King Louis IX of France, informing him that at the king's earnest intercession (through two royal envoys), the pope has admitted the Count of Toulouse back into the grace of the Apostolic See. The operative act is the reconciliation/readmission of the Count of Toulouse (Raymond VII, an unmatched party) to papal favour, brokered by Louis IX. Louis IX appears as the addressee and intercessor whose request moved the pope to act; the Count of Toulouse is the subject of the reconciliation but is not a matched Peerage person.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV grants a privilege to King Louis IX of France (the addressee) exempting him, his chaplains, sworn clerics, and household from incurring excommunication or interdict merely by associating with excommunicated persons, provided they do not share in the crime itself. The document is a one-sided papal indult responding to Louis IX's petition about French prelates and their delegates imposing excommunication on those who associate with persons already excommunicated. There is no live dispute; this is a gracious grant of a personal privilege to the king.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to King Louis IX of France urging him to hand over the regalia to Joffroy (Joffridus), the canonically elected and confirmed bishop-elect of Châlons. The document explains that the transfer of regalia has been delayed due to a procedural dispute involving an appeal by the treasurer of Châlons against the election confirmation. Louis IX appears as the addressee and principal, being asked to perform the investiture with regalia; the bishop-elect of Châlons is the other principal beneficiary. The operative act is the papal exhortation regarding a clerical appointment/confirmation and the delivery of regalia to the newly confirmed elect.

persons: Raimond VII, Comte de Toulouse (subject_or_mention) | Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Innocent IV orders the bishop-elect of Avignon and papal legate Zoen Tencarari to publish in his diocese the absolution of Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, from sentences of excommunication. The absolution was granted at the intercession of King Louis IX of France, with Raymond having submitted to the Church's mandates and provided sureties. Raymond VII is the principal subject of the operative act (absolution from excommunication); Louis IX appears as intercessor. The document is a one-sided mandate, not a live dispute between parties.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Raimond VII, Comte de Toulouse (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, confirming his reconciliation with the Church. The document revokes an unjust excommunication sentence and the characterization of Raymond as a fautor/defender of heretics, issued by Dominican inquisitors Ferrarius and G. Raimundi after Raymond had already appealed to the Holy See. The pope annuls the sentence and any resulting infamy, ensuring no prejudice to Raymond or his heirs. Raymond VII is the sole principal party (addressee/beneficiary); the inquisitors are the counterparty whose acts are being revoked.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Raimond VII, Comte de Toulouse (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV takes Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, his household, lands, and goods under the protection of the Apostolic See. This is a unilateral grant of papal protection (litterae de protectione), with no opposing party named or implied. Raymond VII is the sole addressee and beneficiary of the document.
domain_other_detail: papal protection grant (litterae de protectione) to a lay noble

summary: Pope Innocent IV confirms a sentence pronounced by Cardinal Octavian (S. Maria in Via Lata) regarding the marriage of Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, and Marguerite, daughter of the Count of La Marche. The cardinal had ruled that the marriage could not subsist in law because the parties were related in the third and fourth degrees of consanguinity, and Raymond petitioned the pope to confirm this sentence. The document is a papal confirmation of a marriage annulment/invalidity ruling; Raymond VII (matched) is the principal petitioner/beneficiary, with Marguerite of La Marche as the other principal party (unmatched).

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)

summary: Pope Innocent IV grants a privilege to the consuls and community of Montpellier, at the supplication of those consuls and of King James I of Aragon, providing that the people of Montpellier cannot be summoned outside the king's jurisdiction by apostolic letters unless those letters make special mention of this indulgence. This is a one-sided grant/privilege with no live dispute. King James I of Aragon appears as a co-requestor/intercessor supporting the petition.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Thibaut I (IV), Rey de Navarre (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV writes to Thibaut I (IV), King of Navarre and Count of Champagne, requesting that he take under his royal protection the prepositura of Chableis (a prebend in the church of St. Martin of Tours) held by Simbaldus, the pope's own chaplain and prepositus of that place, as well as Simbaldus's procurator. This is a one-sided letter of recommendation/request, not a dispute. The matched Peerage person, Thibaut I (IV), is the addressee of the papal request.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Innocent IV grants an indulgence to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who visit the royal chapel in Paris (the Sainte-Chapelle), which houses the Crown of Thorns, a relic of the True Cross, and other major relics, on the day of its dedication and its anniversary (one year's indulgence) or during the octave of the dedication (100 days). The document is addressed to King Louis IX of France, who appears as the addressee/beneficiary of this papal grace. There is no dispute; this is a straightforward grant of an indulgence.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (requestor)
summary: Pope Innocent IV instructs the prelates of France not to defend crusade-signed individuals (crucesignati) who commit crimes (theft, homicide, rape, etc.) against secular justice, on the grounds that crusader privileges should not shield criminals. The document was issued at the request of King Louis IX of France (matched), who had brought the problem to the pope's attention. This is a one-sided exhortatory letter with no live dispute; the operative act is the pope requesting financial/military support for Charles's campaign in Sicily via the church tithe. Louis IX appears as the addressee and Charles I of Anjou as the beneficiary of the requested support.

persons: Jeanne I, Reina de Navarre (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to Cardinal Simon de Brion, papal legate in France, urging him to seek loans (from Sienese bankers, the French king, the Count of Poitiers, prelates, clergy, burghers, usurers, and all others) to finance Charles of Anjou, King of Sicily, who is in urgent financial peril. This is a directive letter about securing credit for the Sicilian campaign, not a dispute. The matched Peerage person (Jeanne I of Navarre) does not appear in the document; "rex Sicilie noster filius" refers to Charles of Anjou, not to her — she is a misidentified match and entirely incidental.

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to the entire clergy of France (archbishops, bishops, abbots, chapters, convents) urging them to pay a two-year tithe to relieve the financial distress of Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily, at the request of Cardinal Simon of Santa Cecilia, papal legate. The pope grants an indulgence equivalent to that given to crusaders, and permits the clergy to pledge their benefices for up to three years to raise the funds. This is a one-sided exhortatory mandate with no live dispute; Charles I of Anjou (matched) appears as the beneficiary of the financial relief measure.

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Clement IV issues a mandate to the archbishops, bishops, and clergy of multiple French and adjacent provinces, urging them to pay a two-year tithe at the request of Cardinal Simon of Santa Cecilia (papal legate), in order to relieve the financial difficulties of Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily. This is a one-sided fiscal/crusade-support directive with no opposing party. Charles I of Anjou (matched) appears as the beneficiary of the tithe collection.

This is not a live dispute but a papal appeal for crusade/political finance. Louis IX is the addressee; Charles I of Anjou is the beneficiary mentioned; Alphonse of Poitou receives a parallel letter.

summary: Pope Clement IV writes (for at least the third time) to Cardinal-priest Simon de Brion, papal legate, ordering him to compel all religious orders to pay the tithe in support of the Kingdom of Sicily, using ecclesiastical censure against those who refuse. The document is a papal mandate on clerical fiscal discipline (collection of the ecclesiastical tenth), not a dispute. Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily, is mentioned as the beneficiary of the tithe revenue, explaining why he appears in the matched persons list.

This is an administrative/disciplinary instruction, not a live dispute between parties. Charles I of Anjou appears only as the beneficiary of the tithe collection, not as a party to any conflict.

This is a straightforward papal confirmation of a prior donation with no opposing party named. Ludwig II appears only as the prior donor/grantor, not as a party to any dispute.

summary: Pope Clement IV mandates the bishop of Freising (Conrad) and the bishop-elect of Passau (Peter) to carefully investigate the signs of penitence shown by Otto, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, at the moment of his death. Otto had been bound by various sentences of excommunication for his support of Emperor Frederick II and his son Conrad IV, and as a result his body had been denied ecclesiastical burial. The investigation is to be reported in writing to the Apostolic See so that the pope may proceed on the petition of Agnes, duchess and widow of Otto, and her sons Ludwig and Heinrich. Agnes von Braunschweig is the matched requestor; the Hohenstaufen figures (Frederick II, Conrad IV, Conradin) appear only as background context for the excommunication.

The letter is a piece of political counsel/diplomacy, not a dispute resolution. Charles I of Anjou is the matched Peerage person and the sole addressee.

The document recounts how these three bishops had been recalcitrant during the baronial conflict led by Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, and had subsequently appeared before the pope at Bologna but behaved evasively. The dispute is between the papacy/Holy See and the three disobedient English bishops. King Henry III of England appears only as background context (the king whose realm was in turmoil), not as a party to the ecclesiastical disciplinary action.

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)

The document is a diplomatic letter on the political/ecclesiastical status of Pisa, not a live dispute before the Church. Charles I (matched) is the addressee; Manfred of Hohenstaufen (matched) is mentioned as the enemy whose supporters the Pisans were.

persons: Manfredo I von Hohenstaufen, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV mandates the bishop and official of Paris regarding the absolution of certain Florentine citizens from sentences of excommunication and interdict imposed by his predecessor Urban IV. The sentences had been promulgated because the Florentines supported Manfred of Sicily (an enemy of the Church) and attacked Lucca against papal prohibition. Two named Florentine merchants (Bindus Galligaii and Teglarius Tedaldi) are seeking absolution. Manfred of Hohenstaufen appears only as background context (the persecutor whose support triggered the censures), not as a party to the operative act.

The pope offers Charles the choice of being crowned in person by the pope outside Rome, or in Rome by a delegation of cardinal-bishops, cardinal-priests, and cardinal-deacons, proposing 6 January 1266 as the date. This is a one-sided administrative/ceremonial letter with no live dispute; Charles I (matched) is the sole addressee.

This is a one-sided advisory/diplomatic letter from the pope to Charles, with no live dispute being adjudicated. Now petitions are being made to Charles for the city's rebuilding, while the aggrieved churches and nobles appeal to the king for redress. The pope asks Charles to weigh the circumstances and act as he sees fit. Charles I (matched) is the addressee and principal decision-maker; Conrad IV and Frederick II are mentioned only as historical background to the city's founding.

The pope also presses Charles to address the grievance of King Louis IX of France, who is scandalized by a salt tax (gabella) that Charles levies on French territory. genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Premysl II Ottokar, King of Bohemia (addressee)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to King Ottokar II of Bohemia regarding his planned crusade against the pagan peoples of Galandia, Getvesia, and Letowia (Baltic/Prussian region). The king had requested that, should these territories be conquered, the Archbishop of Salzburg be empowered to elevate the church of Olomouc to archiepiscopal dignity and erect new cathedral churches in the conquered lands. The pope praises the king's zeal but declines to grant the request without prejudice to the church of Mainz (to whose province Olomouc belongs), while encouraging him to proceed with the campaign. The matched Peerage person, King Ottokar II, is the addressee and principal party making the request.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)

summary: Pope Clement IV grants Přemysl II Ottokar, King of Bohemia, the faculty to erect a kingdom in Lithuania (the land of Letovia/Litovia) if he succeeds in wresting it from pagan/infidel hands, and to appoint a faithful person devoted to the Roman Church to govern it. This is a one-sided papal concession/grant to the king, with no opposing party named. The matched Peerage person, King Ottokar of Bohemia, is the sole addressee and beneficiary of the grant, which relates to a prospective crusading enterprise against Lithuanian pagans.

persons: Henry III, King of England (subject_or_mention) | John I 'Lackland', King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius III writes to William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke and Justiciar of England, praising his steadfast defense of the newly crowned King Henry III (crowned by papal legate Cardinal Guala) and urging him to remain faithful to the young king. The letter also condoles on the death of King John. This is a one-sided exhortatory letter — no live dispute is being adjudicated; the pope is simply encouraging loyalty and praising William Marshal's conduct. Henry III and John I appear only as the subjects of the political context, not as parties to any litigation.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)

summary: Pope Honorius III writes to King Henry III of England to console him on the death of his father King John, congratulate him on his coronation, urge him to fulfill John's crusade vow in support of the Holy Land, and exhort him to remain faithful to the Roman Church and follow the counsel of the papal legate Cardinal Guala. This is a one-sided exhortatory letter with no live dispute. Henry III is the addressee; John I is mentioned only as the deceased father whose crusade vow is referenced.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: John I 'Lackland', King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius III writes to the Queen of England (Isabella of Angoulême) to offer condolences on the death of her husband King John I ('Lackland') and to take her under papal protection. This is a one-sided letter of consolation and protection, not a dispute. King John appears only as the deceased husband mentioned in the context of the condolence.
domain_other_detail: papal protection / letter of condolence

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV issues a mandate to all marquises, counts, magnates, podestàs, captains, rectors, councillors, and communes of imperial Tuscany, urging them to keep the peace and obey Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily, as the guardian of that peace. The document addresses the long-standing internal dissensions and factions tearing Tuscany apart, calling on all parties to cease hostilities. Charles I of Anjou is mentioned as the designated peacekeeper to whom obedience is owed, but he is not a disputant — the operative act is a papal exhortation to peace directed at the Tuscan communities themselves.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Henry III, King of England (addressee)
summary: Pope Clement IV grants King Henry III of England a three-year tithe (one-tenth) of all ecclesiastical revenues and incomes in England, Wales, and Ireland, to help him restore order and defend his kingdom after the turbulence of recent wars (the Second Barons' War). This is a unilateral papal grant to the king, with no opposing party. Henry III is the addressee and sole principal beneficiary of the grant.

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to Cardinal Simon of Santa Cecilia, papal legate, concerning a dispute between the bishop of Le Mans and the chapter of Le Mans on one side, and the chapter of Saint-Pierre de la Cour (Le Mans) on the other, over the right to impose an interdict on the city of Le Mans. The underlying occasion was a dissension between the bishop/chapter of Le Mans and King Charles I of Sicily (mentioned only as background context), but the operative dispute is an intra-ecclesiastical conflict over jurisdictional authority to pronounce an interdict, resulting in excommunications being levied against the canons and clergy of Saint-Pierre. Charles I of Anjou appears only as incidental background context, not as a principal party to the dispute being adjudicated.

persons: Philippe II Auguste Capet, Roi de France (requestor)
summary: Pope Honorius III addresses the Archbishop of Tours and the Bishop of Le Mans, revoking the mandate of the Dean of Orléans and other judge-delegates previously appointed to adjudicate claims by those two prelates over the royal chapel of Saint-Pierre-de-la-Cour (Le Mans). The dispute is between the Archbishop of Tours and the Bishop of Le Mans (seeking jurisdiction over the chapel) on one side, and the dean and chapter of the royal chapel (claiming exemption directly under the Holy See) on the other. Philippe II Auguste appears as the requestor who petitioned the pope to protect the chapel's liberty; he is not himself a principal disputant but the royal patron whose intercession prompted the papal action.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)

summary: Pope Martin IV grants an indulgence of 20 days to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who devoutly pray to God for the welfare of King Philip III of France. summary: Pope Alexander IV sends a letter of consolation to King Louis IX of France on the death of his firstborn son Louis (d. 1260). There is no dispute; this is a purely pastoral/consolatory communication. Louis IX is the addressee and Louis de France (the deceased son) is the subject of the letter.
domain_other_detail: papal consolatory letter on death of royal heir

summary: Pope Innocent III writes to Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse, congratulating him on his reconciliation with the Church brokered by the papal legate Milo, and exhorting him to persevere in good conduct. This is a one-sided exhortatory letter with no live dispute being adjudicated; the reconciliation is presented as already accomplished background. Raymond VI is the addressee and matched principal.

summary: Pope Clement IV writes to Cardinal Simon, rector of the Duchy of Spoleto and the March of Ancona, transmitting the text of a letter he received from King Charles I of Sicily reporting his glorious victory over Manfred, former Prince of Taranto (killed at the Battle of Benevento, February 1266). This is a one-sided informational/diplomatic letter conveying news of the military outcome; no live dispute is being adjudicated. Both Charles I of Anjou and Manfred appear only as subjects of the reported news.

persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)

The payment, originally due at the feast of St. Peter but extended to All Saints' Day at the king's request, was duly paid to the apostolic camera. There is no dispute; this is a unilateral receipt/acknowledgment document. Charles I of Anjou (matched) is the paying party whose payment is being confirmed.

summary: Pope Martin IV informs Cardinal John of Santa Cecilia that he has deprived Peter (III), former king of Aragon, of the kingdom of Aragon on account of his occupation of Sicily, his various plots against the kingdom of Sicily, the sedition he stirred up on the island, and his actions against the papacy and the Church. The pope transmits the terms and conditions under which the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona are to be solemnly promised by Philip III, king of France, to one of Peter's sons. The principal parties are the papacy (acting against Peter of Aragon) and the kingdom of France (Philip III) as the prospective recipient/guarantor of the transferred territories; Philip III appears only as the named party to whom the conventions are to be transmitted, not as a disputant himself.

Robert II of Artois appears as one of the two addressees receiving the commission; Charles I, Charles II, and Charles Martel are mentioned as background context for the necessity of the appointment.

Henry VII appears only as the deceased emperor whose death created the vacancy; the real operative parties are the Pope/Holy See versus unnamed persons in Italy who have been usurping imperial vicar titles.

The pope also defends himself against the slander that he wishes to deprive German princes of their electoral rights. This is a political mandate in the context of the German imperial succession dispute between Otto IV and Philip of Swabia. Baldwin IX, Count of Flanders (matched), appears as one of the many addressees of the circular letter; Otto IV (matched) is the subject whose cause is being championed.

John is the addressee/principal; Philip II and Otto IV are the other principal parties mentioned.

The document reflects the broader imperial succession conflict between Otto IV and Philip of Swabia, but the operative act here is a papal mandate/exhortation to the archbishop, not the adjudication of a live conflict.

Otto IV is mentioned as the beneficiary of the required support, not as a direct disputant; the operative conflict is between the pope and the archbishop over compliance with an oath.

This is a one-sided papal commission, not a dispute. Louis IX appears as the subject of the inquiry (the candidate for sainthood), not as a party to any conflict.

Gregory recounts how he processed the True Cross and the heads of the Apostles Peter and Paul through Rome on the feast of the Cathedra S. Petri (22 February), rallying the Roman people to take the cross in defense of the Church, and calls on all recipients to follow this example. The operative conflict is between the papacy (Gregory IX) and Emperor Frederick II; Frederick II (matched) appears as the subject of the invective, i.e., the principal adversary.

The pope requests that the king send a capable representative to work alongside the archbishop of Vienne (papal legate) to resolve the controversies between the prelates and the royal fisc. Louis IX is the addressee and principal party; his father Louis VIII is mentioned only as background context.

Philippe II Auguste is the addressee and matched principal recipient of this letter.

Both parties had voluntarily accepted the arbitration and jointly petitioned the pope for apostolic confirmation. Prior judges had ruled in the deacon's favour, but the provost obtained new papal letters and procedural irregularities ensued, prompting the deacon's appeal to the Apostolic See. Louis, Count of Los is the principal matched party as addressee/beneficiary; Willem I of Holland and Ada of Holland are also matched and central to the dispute.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV mandates Cardinal Simon, legate of the Apostolic See, to convert the hundredth (centesima tax) collected for the aid of the Holy Land, following the counsel of King Louis IX of France. This is a directive concerning crusade finance — the deployment of funds already collected for the Holy Land. Louis IX of France appears only as an advisor whose counsel is to be sought, not as a principal party to any dispute.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (addressee)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily (the addressee), relaying requests from the Duke of Burgundy and Geoffrey, Archbishop of Monreale, who urged the pope to instruct Charles not to engage the Saracens without their counsel and that of the nobles. The pope exhorts Charles to satisfy their wishes. This is a directive/advisory letter to Charles, not a live dispute being adjudicated by the Church. The matched person, Charles I d'Anjou, is the addressee of the papal letter.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Erik V 'Klipping' Christofsson, King of Denmark (addressee)
summary: Pope Clement IV rebukes Erik V 'Klipping', King of Denmark, for allowing and actively participating in the trampling of ecclesiastical liberty in his kingdom, including the ongoing spoliation of prelates and other ecclesiastical persons. The pope urges the king to heed the admonitions of the Apostolic See and of Cardinal Guido (cardinal-priest of S. Laurentius in Lucina, papal legate). This is a disciplinary letter addressed to the king as the principal offending party, with the Church (represented by the papacy and its legate) as the aggrieved party.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Heinrich Markgraf von MeiÃŸen (subject_or_mention) | Agnes von Braunschweig (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Martin IV confirms to the abbess and convent of the monastery of St. Clare of Seußlitz (diocese of Meissen, Order of St. Clare) all the goods and revenues pertaining to their house. The monastery was built by Margrave Heinrich of Meissen on his own land according to the disposition of his late wife Agnes, who had also donated certain revenues to it. This is a straightforward papal confirmation with no opposing party. Heinrich of Meissen and his deceased wife Agnes appear only as the founders/donors whose prior acts are being confirmed.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Hugues de Bourgogne, Vicomte d'Avallon (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Martin IV commissions the Guardian of the Franciscan friary at Dijon (Langres diocese) to dispense Hugh, son of the late Duke Hugh of Burgundy, and Margaret, daughter of the late Count John of Châlon, so that they may licitly remain in their already-contracted marriage notwithstanding their fourth degree of consanguinity. The matched Peerage person, Hugues de Bourgogne (Vicomte d'Avallon), is one of the two principal beneficiaries of the dispensation; his wife Margaret of Châlon is the unmatched co-principal.

persons: Robert II de Bourgogne, Duc de Bourgogne (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Martin IV confirms a composition (settlement agreement) between, on one side, the bishops of Clermont and Auxerre, cathedral chapters, monastic communities, and other ecclesiastical and secular persons of the duchy of Burgundy, and on the other side, Robert II, Duke of Burgundy. This is an active dispute settlement between ecclesiastical parties and a lay ruler over matters within the duchy. Robert II de Bourgogne appears as the principal lay party to the composition.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Edward I 'Longshanks', King of England (addressee)
summary: Pope Martin IV notifies Edward I, King of England, that he has appointed John, Archdeacon of Exeter and papal chaplain, as bishop of the Church of Winchester. This is a routine notification of a papal provision to an episcopal see, with no dispute involved. Edward I appears as the addressee of the notification.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe II Auguste Capet, Roi de France (addressee) | Louis VIII, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Innocent III writes to King Philip II Augustus of France urging him to support the papal legates against the Albigensian heretics in France. The pope exhorts the king to use secular force (the "material sword") to suppress heretics who do not fear ecclesiastical discipline, compelling counts and barons to confiscate heretics' goods and proscribe their persons. Louis VIII (Philip's son) is mentioned incidentally as a possible substitute for the king in leading the action. This is not a live dispute between identifiable parties but rather a papal exhortation/mandate to the king to act against heresy — an operative crusade/anti-heresy directive.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Edward II, King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope John XXII writes to the seneschals of Gascony and Agen informing them of a truce he has imposed between Amanieu d'Albret and Sans-Aner de Pins, two lay nobles, and urging the seneschals to enforce it and work toward reconciliation. The dispute is a live conflict between two lay parties (Amanieu d'Albret and Sans-Aner de Pins) with the Pope acting as mediator/arbitrator. Edward II, King of England, appears only as the suzerain lord of the two nobles and the seneschals' sovereign, not as a principal party to the conflict.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Geoffrey de Mandeville, 4th Earl of Essex (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Innocent III commissions the abbots of Reading and Abingdon and the prior of Wallingford as judge-delegates to hear and decide the complaint of the prior and community of Hurley Priory against the ministers (clergy) of churches on the lands of Geoffrey de Mandeville, founder of the priory, who are unlawfully withholding tithes on newly cultivated land that the priory had previously held when the land was waste. Geoffrey de Mandeville appears only as the named founder of the priory (background context), not as a party to the dispute.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)

This is a one-sided papal grace (marriage dispensation) with no opposing party. Edward I is the matched beneficiary and the direct recipient of the grant.

The document is a clarification of the scope of a dispensation, not a live dispute. Pedro III of Aragon appears only as a named reference point (the deceased king whose descendants are at issue), not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Martin IV grants an indulgence of 20 days to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who devoutly pray to God for the welfare of King Philip III of France. This is a one-sided grant of an indulgence, with no dispute involved. Philip III appears as the addressee and beneficiary of the papal favor.

persons: Conradin von Hohenstaufen, King of Sicily (subject_or_mention) | Charles I Stephen d'Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV issues a solemn bull promulgating a sentence of excommunication against Conradin (Conrad, grandson of Emperor Frederick II), who had been claiming the Kingdom of Sicily and stirring up enemies of the Church against the papacy and Charles I of Anjou, King of Sicily. The operative act is the formal excommunication of Conradin, with a further citation to appear before the apostolic see to answer for his transgressions. Conradin is the principal subject of the censure; Charles I of Anjou appears only as an incidental reference to the party whose interests were being threatened.

persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV writes to Cardinal-priest Simon of Santa Cecilia, papal legate, praising the crusading zeal of King Louis IX of France and promising indulgences to those who take the cross. The pope mandates the legate to diligently pursue the preaching of the crusade and the collection of the tithe in the kingdom of France. This is a directive letter organizing crusade logistics, not a dispute. Louis IX appears only as a subject of praise, not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Jaime II, Rey de Majorca (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope John XXII writes to Philip (Felipe), son of the late King of Majorca and abbot of Saint-Paul de Narbonne, appointing him as bishop of the newly erected diocese of Mirepoix and inviting him to take up its administration. This is a one-sided papal provision/appointment letter with no opposing party. The matched Peerage person, Jaime II of Majorca, is mentioned only incidentally as Philip's deceased father ("clare memorie regis Majoricarum filio").

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Adolf VII van Limburg Graf von Berg (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius IV appoints arbiters to judge the dispute between the city of Antwerp and Adolf, Count of Berg. The matched Peerage person, Adolf VII van Limburg Graf von Berg, is one of the two principal parties to the dispute; the city of Antwerp (an unmatched lay party) is the other.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Edward I 'Longshanks', King of England (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius IV responds to five petitions presented by Otto de Grandson, familiar and envoy of King Edward I of England, concerning the business of the Holy Land (Terra Sancta). The document is a papal reply to crusade-related requests, with Edward I as the principal addressee/requestor. Otto de Grandson acts as intermediary. There is no dispute; this is a substantive engagement with crusade affairs.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Edward I 'Longshanks', King of England (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius IV writes to King Edward I of England urging him to restore the regalia of the church of Meath to Thomas de St. Leger, the elected bishop, which the king had been withholding during the vacancy. This is a one-sided exhortation/grant directed at the king, not a live litigation between two parties before the pope. Edward I appears as the addressee and the party holding the regalia; Thomas de St. Leger (unmatched) is the elect of Meath.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Robert II, Comte d'Artois (addressee)
summary: Pope Honorius IV addresses Robert II, Count of Artois (matched), jointly with Gerard, Bishop of Sabina (papal legate and bailli of the Kingdom of Sicily), explicitly removing from both of them all authority to proceed against Adinulph, Count of Acerra. The operative act is a papal restriction on judicial/administrative action against a specific lay party. The dispute/proceeding is between the papal representatives (Robert and Gerard) acting on behalf of the Roman Church against Adinulph of Acerra, a lay count.

persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius IV grants a 10-day indulgence to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who pray the Lord's Prayer for the soul of the recently deceased King Philip III of France. This is a straightforward one-sided grant of an indulgence, with no dispute or opposing party. Philip III appears only as the subject of the prayers (deceased), not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)

summary: Pope Martin IV grants an indult to Ladislaus IV, King of Hungary, ensuring that the institutions of certain parish priests and rectors made by Philip, Bishop of Fermo (then papal legate), in vacant Hungarian churches under royal patronage — carried out during a period when an excommunication had been promulgated against the king after a legitimate appeal to the Holy See — shall not prejudice the king or his successors in their patronage rights. This is a one-sided papal grant protecting the king's future patronage rights, not an active dispute. Ladislaus IV is the sole matched person and appears as the direct beneficiary of the indult.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Jeanne I, Reina de Navarre (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Honorius IV grants an indulgence of twenty days to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who personally attend sermons held on Sundays and solemn feast days in the presence of Queen Joan of France (Jeanne I of Navarre). This is a one-sided grant of an indulgence to the queen's entourage/attendees, with no opposing party. The matched Peerage person, Jeanne I of Navarre, appears as the beneficiary/requestor of the indulgence.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Robert de France, Comte de Clermont (addressee) | Beatrice de Bourgogne (addressee)
summary: Pope Nicholas IV grants a 10-day indulgence to Robert de France, Count of Clermont (son of Louis IX), and his wife Beatrice de Bourgogne, Countess of Clermont, as well as to all those who attend preaching in their presence. This is a straightforward one-sided grant of an indulgence with no opposing party or dispute involved. Both matched Peerage persons are the addressees/beneficiaries of the grant.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Charles II d'Anjou, King of Naples (addressee)
summary: Pope Nicholas IV grants an indulgence of 100 days to all truly penitent and confessed persons who attend a sermon in the presence of King Charles II of Anjou (King of Sicily/Naples). This is a one-sided grant of a spiritual privilege, with no dispute involved. Charles II is the addressee and beneficiary of the indulgence grant.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Jaime II, Rey de Majorca (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Boniface VIII grants an indulgence of one year and forty days to all truly penitent and confessed persons who visit the royal chapels of James II, King of Majorca, in Perpignan, Montpellier, and the city of Majorca, on specified feast days. This is a one-sided grant of a devotional indulgence with no opposing party. James II of Majorca is the matched beneficiary, as the chapels are within his royal residences.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Jaime II, Rey de Majorca (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Boniface VIII grants an indulgence of 100 days to all truly penitent and confessed faithful who annually visit the chapel of Saint Anne newly built by King James II of Majorca in the castle of Majorca, on the feasts of Saint Anne, the Nativity, Annunciation, Purification, Assumption, and Saint James the Apostle. This is a one-sided grant of an indulgence with no opposing party. King James II of Majorca is the matched beneficiary who requested the indulgence for his newly built chapel.

genre: Titre, général (littere gratiose, cum filo serico)
persons: Jaime II, Rey de Majorca (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Boniface VIII grants an indulgence to James II, King of Majorca, allowing that whenever he attends solemn Mass in any of three royal chapels (in Majorca, Perpignan, and Montpellier) or elsewhere, the preacher may grant forty days' remission of enjoined penances to those present. This is a one-sided gracious grant with no dispute. James II is the sole beneficiary/addressee.

persons: Louis VI Capet, Roi des Francs (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Honorius II issues a solemn privilege confirming the canonical life and possessions of Norbert of Xanten and the canons of Prémontré (Premonstratensian Order), protecting their rule according to the Rule of St. Augustine and listing their churches and properties. There is no dispute; this is a routine confirmation/privilege. Louis VI of France appears only incidentally as a donor of some of the possessions confirmed, not as a party to any conflict. Note: the Analyse mentions the canonisation of Saint Dominique by Gregory IX, which appears to be an editorial error unrelated to this 1126 document.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Raimond VII, Comte de Toulouse (subject_or_mention) | Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory IX writes to the Bishop of Palestrina (papal legate) instructing him to absolve Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, from his excommunications, then notify King Louis IX of France of this absolution, and urge the king to receive sufficient surety from the count that he will join the next general crusade passage with other Ultramontanes and remain in service of the Holy Land for three years. The operative matter is the absolution from excommunication and the crusade obligation imposed on Raymond VII. Both Raymond VII and Louis IX are mentioned as subjects of the instruction, not as disputants.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Manfredo I von Hohenstaufen, King of Naples and Sicily (subject_or_mention) | Conradin von Hohenstaufen, King of Sicily (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X issues a formal process against Ubertinus de Andito, a citizen of Piacenza, declaring that he has incurred the sentences and penalties established by previous popes against supporters of Frederick II, Conrad, Manfred, and Conradin, having persistently adhered to them despite papal warnings. The pope admonishes Ubertinus to return to obedience to the Church before the upcoming feast of the Assumption of the Virgin. The matched Peerage persons (Manfred and Conradin) appear only as background figures whose cause Ubertinus supported, not as parties to the current proceeding; the operative dispute is between the papacy and Ubertinus de Andito.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X appoints Cardinal Simon de Brion as papal legate with full powers for France, the diocese and city of Lyon, and other transalpine regions, primarily in connection with the execution of the crusade decisions made at the Second Council of Lyon (1274) for the recovery of the Holy Land. The document is a commission of legatine authority, not a dispute. King Philip III of France (matched) is mentioned incidentally as the ruler of the realm where the legate will operate.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention) | Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Simon de Brion, cardinal-priest of Santa Cecilia and papal legate, informing him of letters sent to King Philip III of France regarding the crusade effort, and announcing Simon's mission to urge preparation for the sacred expedition. The Second Council of Lyon (1274) had decreed a tithe of all ecclesiastical revenues for six years for the aid of the Holy Land, whose situation is described as desperate (only Acre and two other cities remaining). Philip III and his late father Louis IX are mentioned only as background context for the crusade diplomacy, not as disputants.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Philip III, King of France, congratulating him for having resumed the crusade cross after returning from Africa without completing his vow (along with the army), due to various pressing reasons. The pope rejoices that Philip is now girding himself again for an Asian (Holy Land) expedition. This is a one-sided letter of encouragement, not a dispute. Philip III is the addressee and sole principal matched person.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (beneficiary) | Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Cardinal Simon de Brion, papal legate in France, instructing him to ensure that the tenth (crusade tithe), legacies, and other collections gathered in the kingdom of France are made available to King Philip III of France, who has taken up the cross again for the aid of the Holy Land. The document is a one-sided administrative/crusade mandate, not a dispute. Philip III is the beneficiary of the financial arrangements; his deceased father Louis IX is mentioned only as background context for the earlier crusade effort.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention) | Philippe III, Roi de France (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Gregory X mandates Cardinal Simon de Brion, papal legate to France, to collect crusade taxes (the tenth, twentieth, hundredth of ecclesiastical revenues, legacies, and other funds) from specified dioceses (Liège, Cambrai, Toul, Verdun, Metz) for the aid of the Holy Land, to be handed over to Philip III, King of France. This is a routine administrative/financial instruction for crusade fundraising, not a live dispute. Louis IX (deceased) is mentioned as the original recipient of the grant; Philip III is the intended beneficiary of the collected funds.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X instructs the bishop of Embrun to present himself to Simon, cardinal-priest of Santa Cecilia and papal legate, whenever summoned, and to assist the legate in his dealings with King Philip III of France. This is a routine administrative mandate directing the bishop to cooperate with the legate's mission; there is no live dispute. Philip III of France is mentioned only as the person the legate is to address, not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Louis IX, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Simon de Brion, papal legate, instructing him to collect the tenth (decima) on daily distributions (quotidianae distributiones) just as on other ecclesiastical revenues, in accordance with the decree of the Second Council of Lyon granting a six-year tithe for the aid of the Holy Land. The document is a straightforward administrative mandate regarding crusade taxation, not a dispute. Louis IX of France is mentioned only as a historical reference point (the earlier tithe granted to him by Clement IV), not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Simon de Brion, cardinal-legate, instructing him not to allow or permit the tithe (collected for the crusade/church) to be levied through the clerks of the King of France. The pope acts on complaints raised by prelates at the Second Council of Lyon. The operative matter is the administration and collection of ecclesiastical revenues/tithes, with the legate as addressee and the French royal clergy as the subject of the prohibition. Philippe III of France appears only as the lord of the clerks in question ("clericos regis Francorum"), not as a direct party to a dispute.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X instructs Simon de Brion, papal legate, on how to exhort Philip III of France and other princes of his legation who have taken the Cross to pursue the cause of the Holy Land virtuously — avoiding sin, practicing penance, moderating food/drink/dress, and properly directing crusade tithe revenues. This is a one-sided instructional letter to the legate, not a live dispute. Philip III of France appears only as an example/subject of the exhortation, not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to King Philip III of France urging him to protect the churches and ecclesiastical persons of his realm, and specifically to cease the harassment of the bishops of Paris and Beauvais and the archbishop of Auch, whose churches are reportedly being oppressed by royal agents. The document is an exhortation to the king to respect ecclesiastical persons and institutions. Philip III is the addressee and principal party; the bishops of Paris, Beauvais, and the archbishop of Auch are the aggrieved ecclesiastical counterparties, unmatched in the Peerage.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Philip III, King of France (the matched addressee), asking him to give full credence to Cardinal Simon of Santa Cecilia, papal legate, regarding two matters: compelling by secular force those who contemptuously endure ecclesiastical censure for too long, and making a constitution against monogamists (laymen) who meddle in secular affairs. This is a one-sided papal instruction/credential letter, not a live dispute between parties.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Gregory X commissions Simon de Brion, cardinal-priest of Santa Cecilia and apostolic legate, with a plenary legation in France, the diocese and city of Lyon, and other transmarine regions, primarily for the purpose of organizing aid for the Holy Land following the Second Council of Lyon. The document is a one-sided grant of legatine authority, not a dispute. Philippe III of France is mentioned incidentally as a potential supporter of the crusade cause, not as a party to any conflict.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to Philip III, King of France, to announce that he has entrusted Simon, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia, with the office of full legatine authority (plena legatio). The pope requests that the king provide assistance and favor to the legate. This is a routine administrative letter of introduction/recommendation for a papal legate, with no dispute involved. Philip III appears as the addressee.

genre: Lettre, général (après 1198, littere cum filo canapis)
persons: Philippe III, Roi de France (addressee)
summary: Pope Gregory X writes to King Philip III of France clarifying the terms of the ecclesiastical tithe (decima) established at the Second Council of Lyon (1274) for the aid of the Holy Land. The letter addresses a dispute over interpretation: some are maliciously arguing that the tithe collection should cease if the Holy Land is recovered before the six-year term expires. The pope declares that the tithe shall continue until the Holy Land is fully restored to Christian rule and its retention secured. Philip III appears as the addressee/recipient of this clarification; there is no inter-party dispute being adjudicated.

persons: Thibaut II (V), Rey de Navarre (beneficiary)
summary: Pope Clement IV mandates the archbishops, bishops, and other ecclesiastical persons of the kingdom of Navarre to pay promptly and liberally the tithe (decima) that has been granted to King Theobald (Thibaut II of Navarre). This is a one-sided papal order directing the clergy to fulfill a fiscal obligation to the king; no dispute is described. Thibaut II appears as the beneficiary of the granted tithe.

persons: Eleanor of Provence (beneficiary) | Henry III, King of England (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Clement IV mandates Cardinal-deacon Ottobono of S. Adriano, papal legate, to ensure that 60,000 livres Tournois are paid to Queen Eleanor of England (matched, beneficiary) from the triennial tithe granted to King Henry III (matched, mentioned as the original grantee), in order to settle her debts. This is a one-sided administrative/financial mandate with no opposing party; the operative act is the disbursement of ecclesiastical tithe revenues to the queen.

summary: Pope Clement IV writes to King James I of Aragon requesting that he seize all copies of the Talmud (with its additions and commentaries) and all books of the Jews throughout his kingdom, and have them delivered to the Archbishop of Tarragona and his suffragans. This is not a dispute but a papal mandate directing the king to act against Jewish religious texts. James I of Aragon is the addressee and principal recipient of the mandate.
domain_other_detail: Anti-Jewish religious censorship / confiscation of the Talmud

summary: Pope Alexander III, at the request of Duke Leopold V of Austria, takes the Schottenkloster (Scottish monastery) in Vienna under papal and apostolic protection, confirming all its current and future possessions, in exchange for an annual payment of one gold piece. persons: Premysl II Ottokar, King of Bohemia (beneficiary)

persons: Henry III, King of England (beneficiary)

persons: Willem II Graaf van Hollant en Zeeland (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Alexander IV writes to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, marquises, counts, and other princes of the Holy Roman Empire in Germany, urging them to remain loyal to William II of Holland as King of the Romans and to resist the machinations of those who, while William still lives, are scheming to seize the imperial throne for themselves. persons: Willem II Graaf van Hollant en Zeeland (subject_or_mention)
summary: Pope Alexander IV writes to Archbishop Konrad of Cologne warning him that certain princes, including ecclesiastical ones, are being stirred by malicious scheming to elect a new King of the Romans while William II of Holland (the current king) is still alive. The pope commands the archbishop not to participate in any such machination and declares any nomination, election, or assumption of the imperial dignity by anyone other than William II, while he lives, to be invalid. Willem II of Holland appears as the reigning king whose position is being defended, not as a party to a dispute; the operative act is a papal mandate against an anticipated irregular imperial election.

persons: Henry III, King of England (addressee)
